ORTHOSTATIC TREMOR HERALDING THE ONSET
OF STIFF-PERSON SYNDROME
m
Orthostatic tremor (OT) is a rare, enigmatic, and poorly
understood movement disorder triggered exclusively by
standing, typically with the clinical complaint of unstead-
iness and pathognomonic neurophysiologic characteristic
of 13-18 Hz bursting EMG pattern, i.e., partially fused
muscle contraction.' Abnormal muscle tone control with
stiffness, hyperactive startle responses, and limb spasms
characterize stiff person disorders (SPD), ice., classic stiff
person syndrome (SPS), variant SPS, and progressive
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus.* Auto-
immunity accounts for SPD as a rule,”* and for OT as
an exception.*® Progression of OT into SPS has never
been reported.

cases.text:
Patient 1. A 77-year-old woman developed a disabling
feeling of unsteadiness on standing gradually progressing
over 1 month. Neurologic examination was normal,
except for the presence of a fast tremor of both legs visible
only on standing and quickly resolving on sitting. She
was treated with clonazepam with benefit. After 2
months, lower limb stiffness and spasms progressively
developed, leading to falls, with loss of benefit from clo-
nazepam. Neurologic examination was limited because
of painful spasms induced by movement, emotional
upset, peripheral stimulation, and auditory startle. There
was extreme rigidity of the axis and of flexor and extensor
muscles of the lower limbs and left upper limb with brisk
tendon reflexes. MRI of the brain, cervical, thoracic, and
lumbar spine was normal. Routine hematologic tests and
serum chemistry were unremarkable. Results of antibody
testing revealed anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-
GAD) antibodies in the blood (>2,000 IU/mL),
whereas amphiphysin antibodies were absent. Moreover,
search for an underlying neoplasm with CT of the chest,
abdomen, and pelvis and total body PET revealed no
abnormalities. She was diagnosed with classic SPS and
treatment with IV immunoglobulin (IVIg) conferred sig-
nificant improvement.

cases.text:
Patient 2. A 55-year-old woman presented with a
l-year history of unsteadiness and feeling of “internal
shaking of legs,” only present while standing and com-
pelling her to grope for support. Her medical history was
remarkable for autoimmune hypothyroidism, vitiligo,
and endometrial cancer treated with surgery and

postoperative radiation therapy 2 years before. At neuro-
logic examination, no tremor was visible, but on palpa-
tion of her legs in the standing position a fast tremor was
believed to be present. Surface EMG showed highly syn-
chronized rhythmic EMG activity of around 16 Hz in leg
muscles while standing, completely relieved by sitting
(figure), and a diagnosis of OT was made. She was treated
with clonazepam, which improved the disabling symp-
toms of OT. Four months later, the patient complained
of subacute progressive back pain with stiffness and pain-
ful spasms in both legs. Spasms were more severe prox-
imally, occurred after movement or with emotional stress,
could awake the patient from sleep, and led to multiple
falls with fracture of the right femoral head. The beneficial
effect of clonazepam was no longer sustained. Neurologic
examination revealed exaggerated lumbar lordosis, stiff
ness, and spasms of the lumbar region and lower extrem-
ities. Laboratory tests identified anti-GAD antibodies in
the blood (>2,000 IU/mL), whereas amphiphysin anti-
bodies were absent. Searches for an underlying neoplasm
were negative. She was diagnosed with classic SPS and
treated with IVIg, which removed painful spasms and
partially solved lower limb stiffness.
Discussion. The heralding clinical and neurophysio-
logic findings in our patients were those of OT.’ Sur-
prisingly, in both patients the clinical picture underwent
a change in a short time with progressive stiffness of the
axial and mainly lower limb muscles and painful spasms
resulting in a diagnosis of SPS supported by increased
anti-GAD antibodies and benefit from IVIg.*°
OT is considered to be caused by a central oscilla-
tor. Although cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and basal
ganglia may be involved in OT pathogenesis, it repre-
sents an example of brainstem tremor since brainstem
comprises bilaterally projecting centers, regulating
stance and tone, such as the reticulospinal tract and
pedunculopontine nucleus.’
On the other hand, SPS refers to autoimmune brain-
stem/spinal cord hyperexcitability disorders character-
ized by exaggerated startle, stiffness, and spasms of the
axis and limbs.** Given the information that the tremor
frequency of OT overlaps with the frequency of syn-
chronization seen in the acoustic startle reflex,’ a possi-
bility of a similar generator for both OT and SPS exists.
In this regard, OT observed in our patients can be con-
sidered as a “prodromal and soft sign” of a more complex

brainstem and spinal cord hyperexcitability condition
that gives rise to a progressive alteration of muscle tone,
posture, and voluntary movement and that is potentially
immunotherapy-responsive. Though epidemiologic sur-
vey would be required to confirm a true link between
OT and SPS, pragmatically our observation suggests that
the search also for autoimmunity in a specific patient
with “isolated OT” can be used to prompt for the most
accurate clinical investigation and to choose the most
timely and appropriate therapy.
